subject.title: In Muted Tone
subject.author: Paul Verlaine
subject.text: Gently, let us steep our love In the silence deep, as thus, Branches arching high above Twine their shadows over us.   Let us blend our souls as one, Hearts' and senses' ecstasies, Evergreen, in unison With the pines' vague lethargies.   Dim your eyes and, heart at rest, Freed from all futile endeavor, Arms crossed on your slumbering breast, Banish vain desire forever.   Let us yield then, you and I, To the waftings, calm and sweet, As their breeze-blown lullaby Sways the gold grass at your feet.   And, when night begins to fall From the black oaks, darkening, In the nightingale's soft call Our despair will, solemn, sing.

title: Muted on the Page, Loud in the Concert Hall
standfirst: Verlaine set this love scene inside a painter's borrowed pastoral, then let despair sing through the final line anyway. Claude Debussy composed it twice, and Gabriel Fauré, Raoul Laparra and Charles Martin Loeffler all followed him back to the same twilit grove.

sections.heading: A Poem Four Composers Couldn't Resist
sections.body:
Seventeen lines is not much for a poem to carry, but "En sourdine" — Verlaine's original French title for what appears here as "In Muted Tone" — has been set to music at least four separate times. Claude Debussy composed it twice, once as a student in 1882 and again in 1892 for his song cycle *Fêtes galantes*; Gabriel Fauré set it in 1891; the lesser-known Raoul Laparra and the American-based Charles Martin Loeffler both wrote their own versions later still.

What is striking is how differently they heard the same seventeen lines. Debussy's mature setting chases the poem's hush directly, building deep silence out of long held chords, a static vocal line and repeated pianissimo notes, with the nightingale's call worked in only as a late modulation across registers. Fauré went the other way, favoring visual over aural imagery, using arpeggiated figures to build a warmer, more intimate calm between the two lovers. Loeffler went further still, scoring the poem for voice, viola and piano so that the viola stops accompanying and starts answering, turning the piece into [something closer to a duet](https://interlude.hk/the-music-of-poetrypaul-verlaine-en-sourdine/). Four composers, one poem, four different rooms.

sections.heading: Borrowed Scenery
sections.body:
The poem belongs to *Fêtes galantes*, the collection Verlaine published in 1869, before he had married and long before the wreck that came after. Its poems borrow their cast and their sets wholesale from eighteenth-century painting — Watteau above all, with Fragonard and Lancret behind him — restaging the powdered lovers, masked figures and manicured groves of the *fête galante* genre in verse, using that borrowed decor, as one account of the collection puts it, [to mask personal sentiment](https://interlude.hk/the-music-of-poetrypaul-verlaine-en-sourdine/) rather than declare it.

That borrowing matters for how the poem should be read. Because the lovers in "En sourdine" are dressed in someone else's clothes, from someone else's century, it is a mistake to go looking through the poem for a real woman standing behind it. Verlaine did not marry Mathilde Mauté until August 1870, a year after the book appeared; whatever intimacy the poem imagines under those arching branches, it was invented before he had settled on anyone to imagine it with.

sections.heading: A Poet Already Fluent in Whispering
sections.body:
Verlaine was twenty-five when *Fêtes galantes* appeared, born in Metz in 1844 to a devout Catholic family, an only child who worked a civil service post in Paris while writing. His debut, *Poèmes saturniens* (1866), had made his name at twenty-two despite reservations from some critics, and by *Fêtes galantes* he was already committed to the idea that poetry should work like music before it worked like argument — he later warned against what he called the murderous Sharp Saying, Cruel Wit and Impure Laugh, the kind of pointed cleverness he thought had no place in verse.

"En sourdine" is that ethos at its most disciplined: no wit, no argument, just instruction — dim your eyes, banish desire, let the breeze do the deciding. It is the poem of a young writer who believed, at least on the page, that he knew how to be still.

sections.heading: The Turn in the Last Two Stanzas
sections.body:
For three stanzas the poem does nothing but lower its own volume: souls blending, eyes dimming, arms crossing over a sleeping breast, desire banished. Then, with no warning inside the syntax, it turns. Night falls from the black oaks, darkening; a nightingale calls; and the poem's last line reassigns everything that came before it to a single, quietly devastating verb — "our despair will, solemn, sing." The calm the poem spent its first twelve lines constructing turns out to have been despair's rehearsal space all along.

That late turn is the real difficulty each of the poem's composers had to solve, and it is also the reason the setting cannot simply be pretty. A song that only chases the hush of the opening stanzas is a song that has missed the poem.

sections.heading: The Discipline Didn't Last
sections.body:
Whatever stillness Verlaine could compose on the page, he could not hold in his life. In September 1871 the seventeen-year-old Arthur Rimbaud wrote to him; within a year Verlaine had left his wife and infant son to travel with him through Belgium and England. The relationship ended in Brussels on 12 July 1873, when Verlaine, in a jealous rage, fired two pistol shots and wounded Rimbaud's wrist. He served eighteen months in prison for it, during which he underwent a Catholic reconversion that shaped the more penitential poems of *Sagesse* (1880) and the books that followed.

Read against that record, "En sourdine" looks less like a scene from Verlaine's life than a wish about the kind of man he was not yet failing to be — banish vain desire forever, the poem instructs, two years before he abandoned a wife and child for a teenager he had never met.

sections.heading: Prince of Poets, Dying in the Open
sections.body:
Verlaine spent his last years in the poverty and alcoholism that had shadowed him since the Rimbaud years, moving between hospital wards and Paris cafés even as his early poems were being rediscovered and honored. In 1894, a referendum of fellow writers organized by Maurice Barrès elected him France's Prince of Poets. He died of pneumonia in Paris on 8 January 1896, aged fifty-one, and was buried in the Cimetière des Batignolles.

The hush he wrote at twenty-five outlasted the noise of everything that came after it — still being set to music, still being sung, by composers working long after the man who wrote banish vain desire forever had shown, repeatedly, that he never could.
